    What the AI does here#

    Taskiem uses a language model in four places: to draft a workflow from a sentence (the builder), to diagnose a failed run and propose a fix (repair), to answer one question inside a running workflow (an ai step), and to route chat messages and moderate public pages. The rule from spec 12 runs through all of them: the AI proposes and people dispose. It can draft, diagnose and answer, but publishing, approving, starting a run and reading a secret stay with people, and every proposal goes through the same checks as a person's work.

    • ai765 linesTaskiem's model layer (spec 12.3): one small interface in front of hosted frontier models (Anthropic's Claude by default) and self-hosted open models, so the builder (engine/ai/builder) never talks to a vendor SDK directly.
    • shadow463 linesThe repair pipeline's sandbox (spec 12.2): it forks a failed run's recording into a wd-test case and runs a patched definition against it on the real orchestrator (engine/wdtest), with every task mocked.

    The model layer#

    engine/ai is one small interface in front of every model (decision 0014). A request is system blocks (each can mark the end of a cached prefix), messages, an optional JSON Schema for structured output, a token ceiling and an effort level. Nothing else crosses it:

    ProviderWhat it does
    anthropic (default when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set)Claude through the official Go SDK, claude-opus-5-5 by default. Cached system blocks, effort through output_config, structured output, streaming above 16,000 max tokens, server-side refusal fallbacks unless TASKIEM_AI_FALLBACKS=off, and stop_reason: refusal checked before any content is read (Params).
    selfhostedAny OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions server (vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, a gateway), with response_format: json_schema. Retries a 429 or 5xx three times, honouring Retry-After up to 30 seconds (post).
    fakeA scripted provider that records what it was sent, for tests and the offline evaluation.

    The deployment picks one with TASKIEM_AI_* (ConfigFromEnv). Without a provider, AI building is off and the canvas is the only way to build. Transient says which failures are worth trying again: a rate limit, a 5xx, a timeout or a broken connection, never a 400 or 401.

    The layer turns text into text and holds nothing else. Redacted wraps a provider so every system block and message passes through pii.Redact (emails, phone numbers, BVNs, NINs, card numbers) before it leaves. The builder, repair, chat routing and moderation each wrap their provider themselves, so no caller can forget. AI steps do not use it: they have their own, stronger masking, described below.

    Spec and code differ

    Spec 12.3 says "tenants with strict residency can require" a self-hosted model (spec 12.3). The provider is chosen per deployment, not per tenant: one process has one provider, and every tenant on it uses it. A tenant that needs residency needs its own deployment.

    The builder: from a sentence to a draft#

    A person with workflow.edit types a goal of up to 4,000 characters on the web (POST /v1/ai/build) or in WhatsApp or Telegram. The API records an ai_builds row, reads the tenant's context, and runs the build in the background with no principal at all (startAIBuild). Builder.Build then does this:

    1. Context. aiContext reads names and shapes only: connections by name and connector, data tables by column names and types (never rows), variables by name (never values), roles by how many people hold them (never who), active policies by a summary, the latest definition of up to 100 workflows, of which the builder keeps only the structure, and the published workflows a subflow step may start (those with a manual or subflow trigger, by name and inputs, leaving out the workflow being changed). Keyword scoring picks up to six connectors whose schemas go into the prompt, and up to two templates from the library as starting points (contextDoc). Connectors are passed as manifests with their handlers removed, so nothing in the pipeline can call a provider.
    2. Draft. The model answers an envelope under structured output: a summary, assumptions, the workflow as a JSON string, up to three test cases, or instead a template id and its parameters. The full wd/v1 schema is in the cached system prompt, because the schema itself is recursive and cannot be a strict output schema.
    3. Validate. The draft goes through the same publishing checks as a person's (injected from the API, s.check), then the builder's policy rule: a money-moving connector or capability step with no approval before it is a finding (PolicyFindingsWith).
    4. Correct. Problems and findings go back to the model, up to three times. The budget is checked before each call.
    5. Dry run. The final draft runs on the real orchestrator with every connector mocked from its output schema, plus the model's own cases.
    6. Review. The proposal holds the definition, the problems that remain, warnings, test results, the new data tables it wants, and what it needs before it can run.

    Every model call is written to ai_interactions before its answer is acted on, and a recording failure stops the build. The table is insert-only for the application. Saving is a separate request by a person with workflow.edit: it creates a draft version authored by that person, with the build as co-author in the audit log (saveAIBuildTx). Publishing that draft is the normal publish, with four-eyes counting the saver as the author.

    A build that changes a workflow records the digest of the version it started from (ai_builds.base_digest). If someone saved another version before the proposal is saved, the proposal is merged onto the latest three ways, the base version as the common ancestor, as a canvas save naming its parent_digest is (createVersion). Conflicts come back as 409 with the latest version and digest, and the web panel offers the editor's merge dialog; the save is sent again with resolutions (saveAIBuildTx).

    Resolved

    Saving a build used to write the model's whole definition as the next version with no check that its base was still the latest, so edits saved while the build ran, or before it was saved, were silently undone. The builder's context also had a place for startable workflows that was never filled, so the model was not told which workflows a subflow step could start. Both were found while writing this page.

    Resolved

    Saving from WhatsApp or Telegram sends no resolutions, and a merge conflict there used to fall through as an error, so the person got no reply. The chat now answers that someone changed the workflow since the build started, with a link to make the change on the web; nothing is written, and the build stays a proposal (waBuildSave).

    Spec and code differ

    Spec 12.1 starts from "the canvas, CLI, or WhatsApp" (spec 12.1). The taskiem command has no build command. Telegram, which the spec does not name, has one.

    Self-repair: rules, then the model, then the shadow#

    When a run fails or parks a step, or the drift monitor sees a provider's response change shape, a database trigger queues one repair_jobs row per run and reason, in the transaction that recorded the failure. The failing run waits for nothing. The API works the queue in the background every five seconds, in rounds of one job per tenant, so one tenant's burst of failures does not hold up another's repairs (RepairOnce). A job is skipped when the plan lacks the ai feature, when the tenant turned repair off, or when the run already has an open proposal (decision 0016).

    A burst of failures is analysed once. When the model would be needed, a run that failed on the same version at the same step, for the same reason and with the same class from the rules, is covered by the analysis already standing for it; the job is skipped with a detail naming that proposal. The check holds an advisory lock on the failure, so two workers cannot both start the analysis (sameFailure). Analyses that failed, were interrupted, ran out of budget or were superseded do not count.

    StageWhat happensWhere
    Two views of the runThe history is read twice: opened, for the shadow run, which stays in the API; and sealed, with every envelope replaced by a sample or [category] and free text masked, for anything the model or a stored test may see. Variable values become [variable].Redacted
    RulesError kind, HTTP status, MaybeApplied, drift findings and whether the failing step reads the trigger. Unknown outcome, credential and transient are decided outright and never reach the model.Classify
    ModelAsked only when a patch is needed or the rules are unsure, with the failure, the definition, the redacted run and the schemas of its connectors. Up to three attempts.Repair
    ChecksA patch must keep the workflow's id, change something, pass the publishing checks, and add no policy finding the failed version did not have, compared step by step, with template steps read through the tenant's callable workflows as well as the library.validate
    ShadowThe patch runs on the real orchestrator against the recorded trigger, with completed steps answered from their recorded outputs and everything else mocked. It must complete, send connector inputs that match their schemas, and not change the input of a write the run already made. Then the regression case built from the redacted recording, the model's own test and every stored test of the workflow.shadowCheck, shadow.Run
    FeedbackStep ids, statuses and messages, with every personal value the opened history held replaced, then pii.Redact, then ai.Redacted again on the way out.scrubber

    A patch that never passes is withheld: stored for audit, never offered. Accepting is a person's request (run.resolve, plus workflow.publish for a patch). The patch becomes a new version created by system:ai-repair, published through the normal path. If versions were published after the run's, the patch is first merged onto the latest published one three ways, the run's version as the base, and the result gets the patch's whole check again: the shadow run over the recorded history, which must still leave the input of a completed write unchanged if the patch did, the regression test, the model's test and the workflow's stored tests. The panel says beforehand that the published version will be a merge (published_since), and afterwards shows what the merge changed in the newer version (evidence.merged). A conflict or a failed check answers 409 repair_superseded and marks the proposal superseded. While another repair of the workflow waits for its publish request, accepting answers 409 (rebaseRepair). With four-eyes on, the new version becomes a publish request someone else must approve. The run then resumes as a fork once the version runs in its environment, replaying completed steps and parking any write whose input changed (acceptPatch). An unknown outcome cannot be accepted: the service runs the connector's read-only reconcile action and shows the answer, and a person resolves the step.

    Resolved

    Accepting a repair used to publish the failed run's version plus the fix as the next version, dropping any version published since. Every failed run got its own analysis, so one bad deploy could spend the month's budget hundreds of times; the queue drained one tenant completely before the next; repair ran on plans without AI; and the policy check compared only the number of findings, so a patch that moved an approval from one payment to another passed. All were found while writing this page.

    Risk
    • Data from outside can steer a patch. The model reads the failed run's trigger, which for a webhook comes from outside. The prompt says to treat it as data, and a patch must pass the checks, including the policy check step by step, but the checks cover only what the rules know about, and a patch is one person's click from being published when four-eyes is off. The reviewer's reading of the diff is the real gate.
    • Covered runs are not resumed. Only the run whose proposal is accepted resumes as a fork. The other runs its analysis covered were skipped with a note in their job's detail, have no proposal of their own, and stay failed after the fix is published; a person has to rerun or resolve each of them.
    Resolved

    A patch merged onto newer versions used to get only its own tests again, not the shadow run against the recorded history or the workflow's stored tests, and the person accepting saw only the diff against the run's version. The merge now gets the same check as the patch, and the panel says the published version is a merge and shows its change (rebaseRepair).

    AI steps and personal data#

    An ai step asks the model one question during a run (decision 0050): sort a message, pull fields out of free text, summarise, or draft a reply. It runs on its own ai worker queue, and the worker is the only place a model is called with a run's data (aiEvent). Before anything leaves, the worker:

    1. checks that the deployment has a model, that the business has not turned AI steps off (governance_settings.ai_steps), and that its plan includes the ai feature, through the AISteps.Plan hook the serve command sets from the billing service (AISteps.Plan). A business moved off AI gets a final disabled failure with no model call;
    2. masks the prompt and the input with a Masker: every value the run holds sealed, wherever it appears, in object keys as well as values, and what the detectors recognise, each replaced by a placeholder such as [[name_1]]. The same value always gets the same placeholder, so the model can tell two mentions of one person from two people. Known values of five characters or more are found anywhere in text; those of three or four (a first name such as "Ada", a PIN) only as whole words; one or two characters only when they are the whole value (MinMaskWord). In free text, phone numbers are recognised however they are grouped, by spaces, dashes, dots or a bracketed prefix, and in international form with 8 to 15 digits (detect.go); the builder's redaction uses the same patterns;
    3. leaves as they are only the top-level input fields the step lists in personal_data. Publishing a version with such a step writes ai.personal_data.allow to the audit log, looking inside the callable templates the version pins too (auditAIPersonalData);
    4. refuses a question (the prompt and input together) over 256 KB, the size a step's output may be, with input_too_large;
    5. reserves the tokens the step may use (its question and the longest answer, for both rounds) in ai_reservations, under an advisory lock per tenant, and checks the month's use plus the reservations of steps still calling against the budget, unless the plan bills overage (reserveAI). The reservation is removed when the step is done, and lapses if its worker dies or its call could not be recorded.

    The answer must match the step's output_schema, which is sent with every object closed. A mismatch is sent back once, and a second fails the step with invalid_output. A refusal or a cut-off answer fails it straight away. A rate limit or provider error is retried under the step's retry policy. The placeholders in the answer, in keys and values, are put back, and the output is sealed because it now holds personal values. Each call is an ai_interactions row against the run and step, counted against the budget (recordAIStep). The row is built from the same masked question that was sent, so it shows what the model saw; only the fields let through are redacted in it. If the row cannot be written, the answer is not used, the attempt fails as retryable, and the step's reservation is kept until it lapses, since the provider billed the call. Saving a version with an ai step checks the model, the plan and the switch first, on the definition with its template steps expanded, so an ai step inside a callable template is checked too (aiStepProblems).

    Resolved

    Several gaps here were found while writing this page. The masker replaced values but never keys, so an input built as {name: balance} sent the name to the model, and the interaction log, redacted afterwards, hid it. Known values under five characters were not masked inside text, and only unbroken Nigerian phone numbers were recognised. The worker did not check the plan, so ai steps went on after a downgrade. A call that could not be recorded was still used, unaudited and uncounted. The budget was read once with nothing reserved, so steps starting together all passed, and the question had no size limit. The limit failure said the step would run again, though it was final. And ai steps inside callable templates escaped the save check and the personal-data audit.

    Resolved

    A call whose record cannot be written is still a call the provider bills. Its reservation used to be released with the failed attempt, so the call's tokens were never counted and a database that kept refusing the insert let a step spend tokens on every retry. The reservation is now kept until it lapses, and other steps count it meanwhile (aistep.go).

    Spec and code differ

    Spec 12.3: "hitting the cap degrades to manual building, never to blocking runs" (spec 12.3), and decision 0014: "Hitting it refuses AI building only." Since decision 0050, a run whose ai step meets a spent budget fails. The decision chose this, but neither the spec nor the budget section of docs/ai.md was updated, and that section still promises runs are never affected.

    Chat routing and moderation#

    In WhatsApp and Telegram, a message in a language other than English that the word lists do not recognise can be routed by the model (waModelIntent). It may answer only one of a fixed set of intents with a short argument (Allowed). Yes, no and cancel are not among them, so the model can name a workflow to run but the person still confirms it, matched by the word lists. Routing needs the plan's ai feature; without it, messages are routed by the word lists alone. A build started in chat is the same build as on the web, and it checks the plan too, answering that the plan lacks AI (waStartBuild).

    Storefront moderation asks the model to judge public page text against a written policy after a word list and a price check (ask). Its "allowed" lets text go public, which makes it the one place where a model's answer, not a person's, decides what is shown. The text it judges is written by the business it judges.

    Resolved

    Chat builds, chat routing, repair and ai steps used to skip the plan's ai feature (FeatureAI), which only the /v1/ai routes and saving checked, so a tenant on a plan without AI could build from WhatsApp or Telegram and get model repairs. Found while writing this page.

    Budgets#

    Each tenant has a monthly budget, ai_monthly_tokens (2,000,000 by default, 0 for no limit), summed from ai_interactions for the UTC month. Every token counts, cache reads included. A plan with AI overage lifts it (aiBudget).

    UseCheckedOver budgetOther limits
    Build (web, chat)Before starting, and before each call (aiMeter)429, or the last draft with a warning5 builds per 20 seconds per tenant, 3 per number in chat; 15 minutes; 4 calls
    RepairBefore the job, when the model is needed, and before each attemptSkipped, or withheld15 minutes; 3 attempts; one analysis per version and failure
    AI stepBefore each attempt, counting what running steps have reservedThe step fails for good (limit), and its message says so8,192 output tokens, 2 minutes, 2 rounds per attempt; 256 KB question (input_too_large)
    Chat routingBefore each callNot routed10 per 6 seconds per number; 1,000 characters

    What the AI can never do, and where that is enforced#

    GuaranteeEnforced by
    engine/ai and its subpackages cannot reach the vault, the runtime, the database, the audit chain, ingest, the sandboxes, the shadow, the API or any connectorA test over the import graph that fails the build (imports_test.go)
    Nothing under /v1/ai publishes, approves, starts a run or reads a secretFive routes, compared with a fixed list (TestAIRoutes); a new route fails it
    No AI call has a principalBuilds and repairs run in the background with a tenant id only; their audit entries name the person who asked, or ai-repair with actor type ai
    A proposal is only a draftSaving is a person's request and creates a draft; publishing goes through publishTx and four-eyes
    A repair is never applied by itselfrun.resolve and workflow.publish; unknown outcomes are resolved by a person
    Chat routing never confirmsYes, no and cancel are not intents it can answer
    The AI never approvesVotes need a person's account (Governance and compliance), and no AI path holds one

    Two uses sit outside that boundary by design. An ai step's answer is data the workflow acts on: if an author wires it into a payment, the model's answer feeds the payment, with only the builder's warning about payments without approval, and the builder's rule 21 telling it never to use an ai step for money. And moderation decides what goes public, above. Neither package is covered by the import test: the step's call is made in engine/runtime, and moderation lives in engine/moderation.

    The evaluation suites#

    tools/aieval runs two suites through the same Builder and Repairer the API runs, with the platform's publishing checks and the compiled-in connectors, every connector mocked:

    • Builder (evals/builder): 308 requests in 17 files, each with the connectors, step types, trigger and properties a good answer must have. Properties are small rules over the definition, such as approval_before_payment, idempotency and no_inline_secrets (rules.go). A model judge is optional. TestNoEvalRequestInPrompts fails if any request, or any eight of its words, appears in a prompt or a template.
    • Repair (evals/repair): 22 recorded failures with the class a person expects, whether the rules should decide alone, and a case a patch must make pass.

    Every pull request that touches engine/ai, evals, templates, tools/aieval, api/ai.go, api/repair.go, engine/shadow, engine/pii, engine/wd, engine/wdcheck, engine/expansion or a connector's manifest.yaml runs both suites with the offline heuristic provider against the committed baselines at zero tolerance (ci.yml), and a test keeps that filter covering them (TestCIRunsTheSuitesForTheAILayer). The real model runs nightly when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is a repository secret, and does nothing without it (ai-eval.yml). The heuristic is not a model: it catches regressions in retrieval, templates, validation, the dry run and the grader, not in what a model does.

    Risk
    • No suite covers ai steps, masking or prompt injection. Nothing measures what personal data reaches a model, or whether injected text in a goal, trigger or page changes what is proposed.
    • The real-model gate has never been enforced: there is no repository key (needs-people AI1), and no real-baseline.json to compare with.
    Resolved

    The CI filter used to cover only engine/ai, evals, templates and tools/aieval, so a change to the context, repair, the checks, masking, shadow runs or a manifest moved what the suites measure without running them. Found while writing this page.

    Spec and code differ

    Spec 12.4 asks for "at least 200 real-world automation requests (seeded from dogfooding)" (spec 12.4), and says a model or prompt change ships only if it does not regress. The 308 requests are synthetic, written by engineering and marked as pending review by people. The only gate a change must pass is the offline heuristic, which does not run the model being changed. docs/ai.md still counts 282 builder requests.

    Business modules

    Money log, matching, invoices and receiving money, money reports, Schools, storefronts, forms and data tables: what each is and how it sits on the engine.

    Checked against 0b2999d · 2026-10-28No changes to its code since

    What these modules are#

    Most of Taskiem is a workflow engine. These packages are the products built on it for small Nigerian businesses: a record of the money that moves on their rails, invoices and the matching of money to them, a school's fees, a one-page storefront, hosted forms, and the data tables and files that hold the business's own records. Each is a platform record: its tables live in Taskiem's Postgres under forced row-level security, people change it through /v1, and workflows reach it through a platform connector that needs no credentials (invoices@1, schools@1, storefront@1, form@1). None of them runs inside the engine. They start runs through the ordinary runtime.Start, and they are started by loops in the api role.

    The money log#

    The money log is one row per movement of money on the business's connected rails, and one per later status of it, written once and never changed (RecordTx). What makes a row one movement is its key: the channel, the event and the rail's reference, and for a credit to a customer's permanent account the rail's credit_id as well, because one account takes many credits (Entry.Key). An account credit that comes without a credit_id is not recorded at all, since keyed by the account alone it would hide the account's next credit; the owners are told, once per connection a day, to check it on the rail and enter it by hand if the look-back does not bring it (AlertCreditWithoutID). A unique index on the key makes a payment heard by webhook, by the poller, by a payment step's answer and by the look-back one row. A later status (a payout reversed, a payment returned) is a new row naming the first in corrects, and the reports read each movement's latest row.

    Amounts are kobo in bigint, never floats; a rail's naira amount is rounded to kobo in its manifest (int(math.round(double(...) * 100.0))). The payer's name and account are sealed before the row is written. Rows also come from people: cash and expenses entered by hand (Enter), and bank statements uploaded as CSV, each line keyed by channel, date, amount and reference. A background job copies every row to the business's kept data table money_log in Xenibase, where people read, search and export it but cannot change it.

    One movement of money in can count towards several invoices and orders, a split. Each part is a payment row (customer_invoice_payments or storefront_order_payments), undone by another row, never changed. Both kinds of target count and undo parts through one path, under an advisory lock on the entry (EntryLockSQL, Parts.Count), and a trigger in migration 00210 refuses a part that would make the parts add up to more than the entry counts for, whoever writes it. What an entry counts for is what the payer sent: the amount, plus the rail's fee when the rail settled net.

    Matching#

    Every money-in entry is looked at once (consider), in this order:

    1. Exact, by reference. A payment into a one-time account number or link Taskiem gave for an invoice or an order counts towards it with nobody asked.
    2. Exact, by account. A credit to a customer's permanent account counts towards that customer's open invoices oldest first, then their siblings' where the school shares family credit; what is left is the customer's credit (CountCustomer). A credit whose account number and reference disagree is held for a person.
    3. Exact, by checkout. A payment through a storefront order's Paystack page counts towards the order.
    4. Suggested. Otherwise the 500 most recently sent open invoices and the open orders are scored from 0 to 100 on amount, payer name, reference, date and payers remembered from earlier matches. Up to three scoring 40 or more are offered, each with its reasons. When the business turns automatic matching on, a top score of 85 or more that is at least 15 above the next is matched on its own.

    The three exact rules are skipped for money a person entered (cash entered by hand, or an uploaded statement line) when the business runs a school with a cash threshold: such money is only suggested, so a person matches it (exact). How that match can wait for a second person is under Schools.

    A person confirms or rejects a suggestion, or matches an entry by hand in one or more parts (count). The loop runs every 10 seconds in every api replica; a unique index on suggestions and the entry lock make two replicas looking at the same entry harmless. Money that went back to the payer (a returned payment, a reversed POS sale, a refund that settled) undoes the invoice parts it counted, reopens the invoices, voids their school receipts and tells the owners (reverse). Parts counted towards orders are left, as orders have their own refunds.

    Invoices and receiving money#

    An invoice's status and what was paid are computed by the database from when it was sent or voided, its due date and its payment rows (migration 00197): nothing marks an invoice paid but a payment counted against it (CountPayment). The same payment id counts towards an invoice once while it is not undone, under a second advisory lock on the invoice and payment id. A sent invoice changes only by an amendment with a reason: an added line, a discount, or an item taken out.

    An invoice's page is /i/{token} on the form host, a 24-byte token stored only as a hash. There the customer can ask for a one-time account number or a payment link. The public role only queues the request (taskiem_public_invoice_request, at most 5 an hour and 20 in all per invoice); a one-second loop in the api role issues it on the business's rail (Drain), and a 30-second loop asks the rail whether it was paid (Received). Rails that cannot be asked, such as iswallet, are heard by their webhook alone. A payment counted queues the runs of every prod workflow whose trigger is {"type": "invoice", "config": {"event": "paid"}} or payment, in the payment's own transaction, once per invoice (or part) and workflow (queuePaidStarts).

    Receive money with Taskiem (receive_money.go) gives a business without a rail of its own a wallet under Taskiem's iswallet client, as the connection iswallet/taskiem, so everything above works on it.

    Money reports and the digest#

    moneyreport sums a period from each movement's latest entry: money in and out, settled and pending, by channel, the fees and the effective fee rate, the invoices paid and the leaks. It exports the money log, the invoices and an accounting journal as CSV, with text cells guarded against formula injection. moneydigest sends yesterday's summary each morning from 08:00 Lagos on WhatsApp or Telegram, and last month's on the 1st by email. Each summary is claimed once per business, kind and period in money_digests, in the transaction that queues it, so restarts and several schedulers never send one twice.

    Leaks#

    Every 15 minutes Detector.Tenant runs seven queries per business: money in unmatched after a day, overdue invoices, the same reference and amount twice on a channel, an invoice paid more than it asked, money paid for a voided invoice, a fee above the rate agreed with a connection, and cash a rider owes beyond the limit. A leak opens once per kind and subject, is closed by a person (recovered, written off, not a leak), and closes itself when its cause goes away.

    The duplicate query groups money by channel, direction, reference and amount. For a credit to a customer's permanent account it uses the rail's credit_id in place of the reference, because the reference is the account's and one account takes many equal payments, such as a term's fees paid in two halves (the query).

    Resolved

    The duplicate query used to group account credits by the account's reference, so two equal payments into one student's account opened a "duplicate" leak for money that was not duplicated. This was found while writing this page.

    The look-back#

    For every prod connection that issued customers' account numbers and maps list_credits, every 15 minutes (Every; due connections are looked for every minute), Look reads the last 48 hours of credits back and records each through the money log with the webhook's key, so a credit heard both ways is one entry. A credit the webhook should have brought and did not, more than 30 minutes old, tells the owners once a day that the webhook may not be set up; three failures in a row raise an alert. Who reads a connection is claimed in the database, so two api replicas do not both read it.

    When a read says it was truncated, the window is read again in quarters. If a quarter is still truncated, what was read is recorded, but the run counts as a failure, and three in a row raise the alert (read). list_credits has no pages, so the credits beyond the rail's limit in that quarter are still not read back; the alert is how a person hears of it.

    Resolved

    A quarter that was still truncated used to be only logged, and the run was recorded as successful, so nobody was told that credits were left unread. This was found while writing this page.

    Schools#

    The Schools area (decision 0046) is a school's fees on top of invoices: classes, sessions and terms, students, families and guardians, fee items per class and term, discounts, a term's invoices made once per student and term, account numbers for each student, cash posted at the desk, receipts with a QR check at /r/{token}, a family's page at /s/{token}, reminders and promises, payment plans, clearance at the gate and a daily close. The database keeps its rules (migration 00211): unique admission numbers, one current term, past terms read-only. Students' and guardians' names, dates of birth and phones are sealed under their own subjects, so erasing a person erases them, and kept copies go to the data tables school_students, school_classes and school_term_fees.

    Money reaches a student's fees by one path, the permanent-account rule above. Cash, transfers and POS payments a bursar posts are written as a money log entry (posting:<id>) and counted the same way (PostPayment). The person who asked for anything below can never decide it, with no exception for a one-person school. A second person with school.approve decides:

    • Cash at the desk at or above the school's cash threshold. A posting under it still waits when, added to what money people entered already counts towards the student's invoices without a second person within the window, it reaches the threshold, so postings split under it add up. The window is since the current term was started, and never less than the last 24 hours (SchoolWindowSQL).
    • Money entered on Money and matched by hand. Cash entered at POST /v1/money/entries (or in chat) and uploaded statement lines are the same money. Matching one to a student's invoice when it is at or above the cash threshold, or when it brings the person-entered money on that student's invoices without approval, within the window, to the threshold, records a cash_match request in school_pending_postings and counts nothing (holdMatch, EnteredUnapproved). The API answers 202 needs_approval (matchHeld); approval makes the match as it was asked for (ApproveHeld). Automatic matching never makes such a match. Money a rail reported (its events, the look-back, a step's answer) is never held.
    • Discounts and amendments that lower an invoice. A standing discount at or above the discount threshold waits. So does an amendment to a sent invoice that lowers its total, a discount or an item taken out, weighed by what it takes off. Each is weighed together with what earlier amendments took off the same invoice without a second person and, for a student, with the standing discounts given them and the reductions of any of their invoices within the window (CheckDiscount,RequestDiscountAmendment, ReducedUnapproved). The API answers 202 needs_approval (amendInvoice).
    Resolved

    The cash threshold used to be checked only in PostPayment, so anyone with invoice.manage could enter cash on Money and match it by hand to a student's invoice with no second person, even with the threshold at 0. Taking an item out of a sent invoice was not weighed against the discount threshold at all, and both thresholds were per request, so several requests just below one passed. All three were found while writing this page.

    Resolved

    The totals that stop splitting used to be per invoice (for a desk posting, the student's open invoices), and a standing discount was weighed one request at a time, so payments split across a student's invoices, or several standing discounts just below the threshold, passed without a second person. Both thresholds now weigh per student within the window (EnteredUnapproved, ReducedUnapproved); another student's activity does not count, and a standing discount keeps what it was worth when given (migration 00251). The hold also used to look only at whether the business runs a school, so a hand match to a shop's invoice in the same business waited too; only a student's invoice is held now. These were found while writing this page.

    Storefronts#

    A storefront is a business's one-page public site (decision 0036): a card the owner edits, a catalogue mapped from a data table, actions (order, enquiry, callback, booking), and publishing a snapshot the public host serves. The catalogue's public columns are copied into storefront_catalogue, so page views never reach Xenibase. An order's journey:

    1. The public host checks the form (a signed token, a honeypot, a minimum fill time, proof of work, a rate limit) and writes it, encrypted under a key the api role shares, to storefront_inbox. It cannot seal personal data itself: it has no vault.
    2. The api role opens it, seals the customer, checks prices and stock against the catalogue table, and records storefront_orders. A price that changed holds the order and tells the customer.
    3. An order paid at once gets a Paystack page, checked every 30 seconds and counted when paid at least the total (markPaid), through the same money log entry and parts as matching. Pay by bank transfer on the status page issues a one-time account number as invoices do.
    4. The action's workflow starts with the storefront trigger, deduplicated on the order's id, within the plan's limits (startRun). storefront@1 lets it accept, decline, complete or cancel, ask for payment, notify the customer and refund.

    A business can bring its own domain and prove it with a TXT record at _taskiem-verify.<domain>. The first business to prove a domain serves it; another takes it over only once it is unverified or removed, and every domain is proven again every few hours (VerifyDomain).

    Spec and code differ
    • The spec keeps orders and bookings as rows of orders and bookings data tables in Xenibase (spec 8.1). Both are rows of storefront_orders in Taskiem's database (a booking is an order of kind booking, its slot held in storefront_holds), which is what lets them take part in matching and the money log.
    • Spec 7.5 has submission limits per page and per hour with alerts, per phone number on orders, and 100 a day per IP (spec 7.5). The code has a bucket per IP hash only, 20 every 10 minutes (SubmissionsPerIP), and the plan's run limits behind it. formguard's comment says per-page and per-phone limits "sit on top"; none exist. The optional phone code on orders is not built.

    The public host and its isolation#

    publicweb serves storefronts, hosted forms, invoice pages, receipts and family pages to anyone. It runs as the public role, apart from the API and the edge, with its own database login and a pool of five connections (TASKIEM_PUBLIC_DATABASE_URL). That login is taskiem_public, which reads no table at all: it may only execute SECURITY DEFINER functions (38 are defined across the migrations) named taskiem_public_*, owned by taskiem_dispatch, each of which takes a host, a token's hash or a reference with its key and answers only what a page shows.

    Isolation between businesses rests on three things, and each held where it was checked:

    • The host decides the tenant. A request's host is looked up once (DBLookup, cached 30 seconds, misses 10), and every storefront page then reads by that site's id. Status pages, payment, rating and change pages read an order by reference and its status key, and refuse one whose storefront is not the host's (statusOf), so a reference from another shop answers "not found".
    • Tokens, not ids, on the form host. Invoice, receipt, family and form-link pages are reached by 24-byte random tokens stored as hashes; a malformed, unknown and expired token answer the same page. Each function also checks the tenant is active.
    • Writes are requests. The public role never writes a tenant's record. It queues: an order in storefront_inbox, a submission in form_inbox, an account-number request, a family's "I have paid" or plan request in school_family_inbox, each with its own limits counted in the database (taskiem_public_school_family_ask: 5 claims an hour, 3 plan requests, 3 new links), and the api role does the rest.

    Every response carries the public security headers, with frames allowed only under /embed/ and only from the business's verified websites; any cookie a handler tries to set is dropped and logged (cookieless). Page views are limited to 300 a minute per address, form submissions to 20 every 10 minutes on storefronts and 50 an hour on the form host, and "Report this page" separately. TLS certificates for businesses' domains are issued only for hosts that serve (TLSAsk).

    Spec and code differ

    The spec has cache misses "read the read replica, not the primary" (spec 8.4). The public host connects to TASKIEM_PUBLIC_DATABASE_URL, which defaults to the primary; a replica is the operator's choice.

    Forms#

    A hosted form (decision 0037) is either a workflow's trigger, {"type": "form"} on forms.<domain>/f/{id}, or a form step that waits for a person: a member in the app, or an outsider through a one-time link (/r/{token}) with an optional code by SMS or email. The form host checks each page and seals what it receives for the api role; Process checks it again against the deployed version's schema, keeps files in the business's private Xenibase bucket, seals the fields the schema marks personal and anything that looks personal, records form_submissions once per reference, and starts the run or answers the step. Files are read back only through signed URLs, by a person with pii.reveal or a form@1 step.

    Spec and code differ

    The spec limits submissions "per form and per IP hash" (spec). There is a limit per IP hash only (FormSubmissionsPerIP), and the organisation's ingest limits.

    A member's list of form steps waiting for their roles is filtered by those roles in the query, owners seeing every role's, newest 100 first (>'role' = ANY($2)">listFormRequests).

    Resolved

    The list used to read the 100 newest pending requests of any role and filter by role afterwards, so in a business with more than 100 waiting for other roles a member saw none of theirs. This was found while writing this page.

    Data tables, on Xenibase#

    Data tables (decision 0033) are a business's own records, such as customers, stock and staff, kept as Postgres tables in a Xenibase project, one project per organisation. Taskiem keeps the definitions (data_tables, data_table_columns) and the project's state; the rows live only in Xenibase. The first table provisions the project; schema changes go through Xenibase's preview and apply, never SQL text Taskiem writes; and the connection's token is renewed before it expires. Workflows reach the rows through the ordinary xenibase@1 connection named data_tables in prod, and the API through the same connector's actions, so this package never sees a row.

    Some tables are kept by Taskiem: money_log, money_matches, school_students, school_classes, school_term_fees. Their rows are copies only Taskiem's own writers add. The page, the rows API, chat and the storefront refuse to change them, and the worker refuses a write step that names one, or any call_function on the project while it keeps a table (GuardStep). A business that brought its own project can still edit them in Xenibase; since the records are copies, that changes no money.

    Media#

    media stores a business's files in its Xenibase project's storage, in two buckets. The public one holds storefront photos: decoded only after the header says at most 25 million pixels, turned upright, stripped of metadata, stored at fixed widths under content-named paths and cached for good. The private one holds form uploads (JPEG, PNG and PDF up to 25 MB), reached only through signed URLs that last at most seven days. Taskiem uses the project's API token through Xenibase's management API, so no storage policy is needed and none can open them.

    How tightly each sits on the engine#

    The modules are loosely coupled to the runtime and tightly coupled to each other. None is in the engine's packages, none changes how a run executes, and each reaches runs only by runtime.Start, a signal to a waiting step, or a platform connector. Their loops all run in the api role (runInvoicePayments: requests every second, payments every 30 seconds, matching every 10, leaks every 15 minutes; runSchoolAccounts: account batches every 2 seconds, and the look-back, which checks every minute for connections due and reads each one every 15 minutes). Between them the coupling is deliberate: Schools is invoices plus records; invoices, orders, cash postings and the look-back all count money through the money log's one path; and the public host only reads published pages and writes requests the api role picks up.

    Part E · Product modules

    Web app

    The builder canvas, run inspector, operations pages and embedded builder: structure, state, and how they talk to the API.

    Checked against 09b5e6a · 2026-10-28
    The code has moved: 4 commits since
    • api/workflows.go
    • web/e2e/editor-json.spec.ts
    • web/src/lib/keep.test.ts
    • web/src/lib/keep.ts
    • web/src/pages/Editor.tsx
    • web/src/pages/RepairPanel.tsx

    What it is#

    The web app in web/ is everything a person sees of Taskiem in a browser: the console a business works in (workflows and their builder, activity and the run inspector, approvals, money, storefront, schools, settings), the operator console at /ops, and a second bundle that partners put on their own pages to give their customers a builder. It is one React app, about 60,000 lines of TypeScript, with no server of its own. The Go binary serves the built files, and every piece of data comes from the same REST API that the CLI and the SDK use.

    Structure and routing#

    PathWhat it holds
    main.tsx, App.tsxThe entry point and the shell: sign-in gates, the sidebar, the phone tab bar and every route
    PageBoundary.tsxThe error boundary around the routes, which keeps one page's failure to that page
    api.ts, auth.tsxThe API client and the signed-in person
    pages/One file per screen, about 25,000 lines. Editor.tsx is the builder, Run.tsx the run inspector, MergeDialog.tsx the dialog both the builder and the AI build panel use to settle conflicting saves
    builder/, canvas/The canvas, the step picker, a step's window and its settings panel, trigger editors, the run canvas
    forms/Fields generated from JSON Schema, pickers, and the form a respondent sees
    lib/Pure functions behind the pages (the canvas model, timelines, money, plain words, the unsaved-changes warning), each with its unit tests
    embed/The embeddable bundle: custom elements, its own client and the frame protocol
    ops/The operator console, loaded only under /ops
    e2e/Playwright specs against the real binary

    The entry point picks one of two apps by path, before React mounts anything. The operator console has its own session cookie and its own client (opsApi), and it never mounts the tenant console's providers:

    Inside the console, routing is react-router-dom 7 with a BrowserRouter. Shell decides what a person may see before any route is matched. While /v1/me is loading it shows a skeleton. Signed out, every path but signup and password recovery goes to /login?next=…. Someone with only invitations, an administrator who must still enrol a passkey, and a school gate account each get one screen whatever the address. A field agent lands on the agent app, and while they work in a business the pages render inside that business's session. Everyone else gets SignedIn: the sidebar, filtered by permission, and about 70 routes in one <Routes>, wrapped in PageBoundary. A page that throws while rendering shows "This page stopped working" with Try again and Go to Home, and the sidebar and the rest of the console keep working; since the page container is keyed by the path, moving to another page starts afresh. A workflow's own page switches the shell to builder mode, which shrinks the menu to a rail of icons.

    Pages are imported eagerly; only the operator console is a lazy chunk. The page container is keyed by the path and a refresh counter, so pull-to-refresh in the installed app redraws the page and every page fetches its data again.

    Framework and build#

    React 19, TypeScript 6 in strict mode with noUncheckedIndexedAccess, Vite 8, and React Flow (@xyflow/react 12) for the canvases (package.json). There is no state library, no CSS framework and no component kit. Styles are one stylesheet of CSS variables, styles.css, and the rules for using them are in Building screens in Taskiem's look. Types for workflow definitions come from the SDK through a path alias, @sdk/wd, so the console and the SDK share one wd/v1 type.

    pnpm --filter @taskiem/web build type-checks, then makes two builds. The console goes to dist/. The embed bundle is a library build of src/embed/index.tsx into one classic script with its styles inlined:

    taskiem serve serves dist/ from TASKIEM_WEB_DIR through SPA: a path that is not a file gets index.html with no-cache, so client routes survive a reload; hashed assets are cached for a year; /v1/ and /hooks/ never fall through to the app. Every response carries the console's Content-Security-Policy, which allows scripts only from the console's own origin and no inline script (httpsec.CSP). In development, Vite proxies /v1 and /hooks to :8080 so the session cookie stays same-origin.

    State#

    State lives in components. Three small pieces are shared:

    • AuthProvider holds the result of /v1/me: roles, permissions, the Advanced switch, and flags such as gate_only. can(perm) reads the permission list. Inside a field agent's session, AgentPermissions replaces can with what the agent may do in that business.
    • useLoad fetches on mount and when its dependencies change, ignores an answer that arrives after unmount, and, with poll, fetches again every 2 seconds. Every page loads its data with it. useAction runs a button's work with a busy flag, an error and a toast.
    • The agent's business session is module state in api.ts, kept in sessionStorage for the tab and read with useSyncExternalStore.

    Nothing secret is kept in browser storage. localStorage holds the theme, the brand, whether More is open in the menu, and which consent screens a field agent has seen. sessionStorage holds the agent session's id and kind, the page to return to after an OAuth connection, and a gate's recent checks. Tokens that arrive in links (password reset, signup, invitation, operator enrolment, a WhatsApp step-up hand-off) are read from the URL fragment, which the browser does not send, and all but the hand-off are then removed from the address bar.

    Talking to the API#

    Every call goes through one function. It sends the session cookie (credentials: "same-origin"), always adds X-Taskiem-Request: 1, adds the agent header when the agent is working in a business, and turns an answer that is not 2xx into an ApiError carrying the status, the message, the validator's problems and the whole body:

    A request the browser could not send at all becomes status 0 with a plain offline message. A 401 outside /v1/auth/ fires taskiem:unauthorised; the auth provider sets the person to signed out and the shell sends them to the login page. Pages show errors with ErrorBox, and the validator's problems with ProblemLine, which links each to the step that needs fixing. Creating and sending invoices use postOnce, which sends an Idempotency-Key so a retry makes nothing twice.

    The session is an HttpOnly cookie, SameSite=Lax (setSessionCookie). A browser's sign-in gets the cookie and no token in the body, which decision 0026 settled. The CSRF defence is the header: the API refuses any request authenticated by the cookie that is not a GET or HEAD and lacks it. A cross-site form cannot set a header, and a cross-site fetch with one needs a preflight the API does not grant. Sign-in itself takes only application/json (jsonOnly), which a cross-site form cannot send either.

    Hiding what a person may not do is only for the screen. can() filters the menu and turns off buttons, but each route checks the same permission on the server, for example s.need(PermWorkflowEdit) on saving a version and s.need(PermWorkflowPublish) on publishing (server.go).

    The builder and how it edits wd/v1#

    The builder (Editor) loads the workflow, the version in ?v= (else the latest), the connector catalogue and the capabilities, and keeps the definition being edited in component state with a dirty flag. A draft saved without a trigger, which drafts may be, opens as a manual one (Editor.tsx). Its tabs are Build, Runs and Settings, and with Advanced on, Code (the workflow as SDK TypeScript, compiled by the API) and JSON.

    The canvas model is lib/flow.ts: pure functions over the definition, unit-tested without a browser. A step inside a container is addressed by the list it is in:

    flowGraph turns the definition into cards and arrows at every depth, with a place for the first step of an empty path and for what follows a container. Positions saved in the layout win, and the rest are placed in columns by the longest path from the trigger. Every edit the canvas makes is one function that returns new steps:

    EditWhat it does to the definition
    insertStepAdds a step after one, before one, or between two, rewriting needs so the chain stays joined, and places it next to its neighbour in the list
    removeAnywhereRemoves a step and what it holds; the steps that needed it now need what it needed
    connectInAdds "target needs source" only within one list, and refuses a loop
    renameAnywhereRenames a step and the needs in its list. Expressions that name it are not rewritten; the validator reports them
    forSavingBefore saving, drops a choice's empty "otherwise", since wd/v1 lists hold at least one step

    New step ids come from the picker's base word, unique across every depth (idFrom). Undo and redo keep the last 50 definitions with their layouts.

    Typed JSON reaches the definition only once the builder can draw it. The JSON tab applies a value only when definitionProblem finds nothing wrong with it: an object with a trigger and a list of steps, each an object with an id and a type, with the same shape inside every container. Otherwise it says what is wrong and keeps the last definition that worked. A step's "Edit this step as JSON" goes through stepFromJson, which applies the same check and refuses a change to the id. Renaming is done in the ID field, which checks the id is free at every depth and rewrites the needs that point at the step.

    Every save is a new immutable version. The builder sends the digest of the version it started from, and when someone saved since, the API merges the two edits three ways; units both changed come back as a 409 with the conflicts, and the merge dialog asks which side to keep:

    The AI build panel saves the same way and opens the same MergeDialog, with the AI's proposal in place of "Yours".

    On the server, createVersion locks the workflow, refuses one Git manages, merges with wdmerge and stores the result; it answers with the validator's problems but saves the draft whatever they are, as long as it is a wd/v1 shape: draftDoc applies the rules of definitionProblem except the trigger, which a draft may lack: an object with a steps list, each step an object with an id and a type, with the same shape in every If's paths and otherwise, every parallel's branches and every for-each's steps (draftSteps). It reads the body as maps, where keys match exactly, and refuses a top-level wd/v1 key spelled in another case, such as "Steps". Publishing validates. Moving cards does not make a version: the layout is PUT on the current version 600 ms after a drag, and only while there are no unsaved edits, as spec 3.5 asks (spec 3.5). Publishing saves first, then publishes; a version that is not ready comes back as a list of needs, each with its fix, and with four-eyes on it waits for a second person.

    While there are unsaved edits, useLeaveWarning asks before they are lost: closing or reloading the tab gets the browser's own question (beforeunload), and a click on a link to another page of the console, the back link and the menu among them, asks "Leave without saving?". The router is a plain BrowserRouter, which cannot block navigation, so links are caught as they are clicked.

    What a click cannot catch, the browser's Back button, a 401 that signs the person out, a closed tab, is covered by keeping the edits: while there are any, the builder keeps the definition, the layout and the version they were made on in the tab's sessionStorage, keyed by workflow (keepDraft). Opening that workflow again offers them back, "You have changes to this workflow that were not saved", with Bring them back or Throw them away. Brought back, they save against the version they were made on, so a version saved since is merged as usual. Saving, throwing them away or discarding them for another version forgets them. Storage that is missing or full is ignored, and the builder works without it.

    Resolved

    The JSON tab used to apply any JSON object as the definition on every keystroke, and with no error boundary a definition without steps blanked the whole console and lost the edits; the API stored such a draft too, blanking the builder for everyone who opened it. Editing a step as JSON renamed it on the first keystroke without checking the id or rewriting needs, and nothing asked before leaving the builder with unsaved changes. All three were found while writing this page.

    Resolved

    The browser's Back button used to leave the builder and drop the edits without asking, since it changes the history without a click on a link, and a 401, which signs the person out, dropped them too. This was found while writing this page.

    Resolved

    Below the top level the server used to take any JSON as a draft, and draftDoc, decoding into a struct, took "Steps" for steps. A draft saved through the API with only "Steps" could not be drawn, and one with a malformed container might not be: the builder for that workflow then showed "This page stopped working" until a good version was saved. This was found while writing this page.

    The run inspector#

    RunPage reads a run's whole history once from GET /v1/runs/{id}, then, while the run is not finished, streams the events recorded after the last one it has, by server-sent events, and fetches the run again when the stream ends:

    timeline folds the events into one row per step instance (pay_all[2].pay_employee): status, attempts, input, output, logs, error, and what a waiting step waits for. The page shows those rows as cards or on the run canvas, with each step's plain-words error, the secrets and connections it decrypted (for audit.read), the form answers that started it, and the run's forks and subflows. Sealed personal data is shown as 🔒 by redact; the values are not in the browser unless revealed. Cancel (with or without reversing what the run did) and resolving a parked step are posts to the run, behind run.cancel and run.resolve.

    Ticking "Reveal personal data" (pii.reveal) fetches the run once with ?reveal=true. The stream is sealed, so while personal data is shown a live run is not updated: the page says so and offers Refresh, which fetches it again. Unticking goes back to the sealed history and its stream:

    On the server, auditRevealOnce writes one pii.reveal entry to the audit chain per person and run in any 10 minutes, so a page that fetches a revealed run again does not write an entry each time.

    A failed run that the AI has analysed shows its repair in RepairPanel. Accepting it merges the fix onto the latest published version; when a version published since changes the same parts, or the proposal's tests fail on the result, the API refuses with a 409 and marks the repair superseded. The panel reloads after a refused decision too, so it then says the fix can no longer be applied and asks for one by hand.

    Resolved

    A revealed live run used to be polled every 2 seconds, and each fetch wrote a pii.reveal entry, so a tab left open on a waiting run wrote 1,800 entries an hour and buried the pii report. This was found while writing this page.

    Forms and the builder#

    A step's settings are drawn from what its connector declares. SchemaForm turns an action's input JSON Schema into fields: text, numbers, booleans, enums and nested objects, each of which can also take an =… expression or a value picked from an earlier step. A schema without properties falls back to a JSON box. What a step can pick from is worked out at every depth, the steps before it in its own list and in each list it sits inside (earlierAnywhere), with samples once the draft has been tested. "Test workflow" posts the draft to /v1/workflows/{id}/try, which runs it with sample data and sends nothing; outputs can be kept for the next test.

    A step opens in StepWindow, full screen: what came in, its settings (StepPanel), and what came out. Form triggers and form steps get FormEditor: fields with their personal-data categories, pages, and a live preview drawn by FormView, the same component members fill forms in with at /forms/:id and /forms/requests. Public forms are not this app; the public host serves them.

    Nowhere does the app put markup from data into the page: there is no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML or markdown renderer anywhere in web/src, so run outputs, connector schemas and form answers are always text. Links taken from data (a Git pull request, a provider's confirmation link, a notification) go through React 19, which blocks javascript: URLs.

    The embed bundle#

    /embed/v1/taskiem.js defines three custom elements (embed/index.tsx). <taskiem-builder> and <taskiem-runs> run on the partner's page. <taskiem-frame> is the root of the frame page, for partners who prefer an iframe. Each renders into its own shadow root with the console's stylesheet scoped to :host, so neither page's styles reach the other. The partner's colours, font, radius and logo become CSS variables only after parseBranding has checked each against a pattern, so branding cannot inject CSS.

    The bundle has its own client, EmbedClient. It calls only /v1/embed/{app}/… on the origin the script came from, sends the end user's token as a bearer header with credentials: "omit", so the console's cookie never goes with it, and streams runs with fetch, because EventSource cannot send a header. It warns the host page a minute before the token expires; only the partner's server can mint the next one, which the page hands over with setToken.

    In iframe mode the token travels by postMessage, never in the URL. The frame announces itself to the parent, and accepts a token only from its parent window, only from one of the app's origins, and once it has one, only from that origin. It posts back only to that origin, never to "*":

    The server holds the other half. embedFrame serves the frame page with frame-ancestors set to the app's origins, excluding Taskiem's own, and a policy that keeps scripts and API calls on its own origin (FrameCSP). Every other page sends frame-ancestors 'none'. embedCORS answers CORS only for the app's exact origins, without credentials. embedAuth requires a token whose audience is the app in the path, from an allowed origin and the token's bound origin if it has one; a request without an Origin is accepted only for a headless app. From the frame page, which runs on Taskiem's origin, the origin that counts is the partner page named in X-Taskiem-Embed-Parent (embedOrigin). Definitions an end user saves or validates go through embedGuardBody, which refuses connectors, step types and templates the app does not allow (embed.Uses); publishing and starting a run check the stored version again. The guard reads the body as a map, where keys match exactly, while the handlers decode it with encoding/json, which matches field names without regard to case, so it refuses a definition or template key spelled in any other case (embed.go).

    The embedded builder is not the console's builder. It draws top-level steps only, with lib/graph.ts, the model the console used before flow.ts, has a palette of step types instead of the picker, and edits nested steps as JSON in their parent's panel. The run view, the run canvas and the step panel are shared with the console; the panel reads permissions from EmbeddedAuth, which gives it the end user's permissions with the technical parts shown, since the bundle has no console session. Renaming a step refuses an id taken at any depth (freshId). A save sends parent_digest, and a 409 with conflicts opens an inline choice between the end user's edit and the newer version's, with the edits left on the canvas.

    Resolved

    An end user who sent "Definition" used to skip the save guard and store a draft with steps or connectors the app does not allow, against what decision 0015 and the partner guide say. The embedded builder's rename checked only top-level ids, and a conflicting save showed only an error, so the end user had to redo their edit. All were found while writing this page.

    Tests and how CI runs them#

    KindWhatWhere it runs
    Unit (Vitest)61 files and about 580 tests, all over pure modules: lib/ (the canvas model and definitionProblem, timelines, money, forms, plain words, which link leaves the page), builder/, the embed client's SSE parser, expiry timer and frame checks (embed.test.ts). No component is rendered: there is no DOM environment (vitest.config.ts)pnpm test in CI's typescript job, with lint and type-check
    Browser (Playwright)44 specs, about 80 tests, in Chromium against the real binary. serve.sh builds it with -tags e2e, makes a fresh database, a partner tenant, an operator, a demo school and fake WhatsApp, SMTP, Termii and iswallet servers, and serves every role. embed.spec.ts runs a partner page on another origin with the element and the iframe, and the embedded builder's rename and conflicting save. run-inspector.spec.ts reveals a live run's personal data and resolves a parked step; editor-json.spec.ts covers the JSON tab, a draft without a trigger, the error boundary, the leave warning, edits kept through Back and a sign-out, and a step edited as JSONCI's web job, on every pull request: build, install Chromium, pnpm e2e; traces kept on failure
    Accessibility (axe)axe() injects axe-core and checks WCAG 2.2 AA and best practices. accessibility.spec.ts checks 47 pages (/home among them), a term's fees and invoices, a waiting run's page on its canvas and its timeline, and the builder's dialogs, in the light and the dark theme; 21 other specs check the pages they openPart of the Playwright run
    Risk

    Everything that is not a pure function is tested only through Playwright: the 25,000 lines in pages/, the builder's state, the editor's save and merge, the JSON tab, useLeaveWarning beyond leavesPage. The embedded builder's editing is covered by two tests, and its save guards from the browser's side by none; the case-variant refusal is tested only in Go.

    Resolved

    No spec used to open the run inspector's reveal or resolve a parked step, and no spec ran axe on /home or /runs/:id, though the web app's own rules say every page passes axe. Both were found while writing this page.

    Where the documents have moved on#

    Spec and code differ
    • The web app's README says the canvas shows top-level steps and that there is no live run view. The console's canvas shows steps at every depth, and the inspector streams a running run. Its list of limits describes the embedded builder.
    • Spec 15.1's live view lights steps "on the canvas as a run executes" (spec 15.1). The run canvas draws only top-level steps (RunCanvas); a container's card takes the state of what it holds, and the steps inside are seen only on the timeline.
    • Spec 15.1's search finds runs "by correlation key, status, date, or a redacted field value" (spec 15.1). Activity filters by status, workflow, environment and the end of a date range on the server; the start of the range and its search box work on the runs already loaded, 50 at a time, and the search matches workflow, run id and who started it. There is no search by correlation key or field value.

    Part Z · About

    How the atlas is maintained

    Where the atlas's pages live, how the build reads the code, how to tell which pages the code has moved under, and how to update and publish it.

    What it is made of#

    The atlas lives in docs/atlas next to the code it describes, so a change to one can come with a change to the other in the same pull request.

    PathWhat it is
    pages/*.htmlOne file per page: a JSON header, then the page's HTML. The file name only sets the reading order on disk. The header's part and order set the order in the atlas.
    partials/*.htmlDiagrams used on more than one page or too long to keep inline. {{uid}} in a partial is replaced each time it is included, so marker ids never clash.
    src/The shell, the stylesheet and the page script that every page shares.
    atlas.jsonThe title, the repository URL that code links point to, and the parts.
    atlas.mjsThe build. Node 22 and git, no packages.
    site/index.htmlThe built atlas: one self-contained file. Open it from disk or serve it anywhere. It is committed, so reading it never needs a build.

    A page's header#

    Every page starts with a comment holding JSON:

    • verified is the commit the page was last checked against, line by line. Set it only after reading the code at that commit.
    • sources are the files and directories the page describes. A commit that touches any of them after verified marks the page as moved.
    • status: "planned" with a scope list renders a placeholder that says what the page will cover.

    Elements that read the code#

    The build replaces these elements before writing the page. Anything that names code is resolved against the working tree, and links are pinned to the commit that was built.

    ElementBecomes
    <x-ref path="…" symbol="…">text</x-ref>A link to the first line in the file containing symbol. Without symbol, a link to the file. A path ending in / links to the directory.
    <x-code path="…" start="…" [end="…" | lines="n"] [doc] [max="n"] [caption="…"]/>An excerpt with highlighting and line numbers. It starts at the first line containing start and runs to the line containing end, or for n lines, or by default to the brace that closes the block. doc includes the comment above it.
    <x-packages names="a,b"/>, <x-packages rest/>Package cards with size and doc comment, read from the code. rest lists every engine package that no other x-packages mentions, and the build reports it.
    <x-stat name="…"/>A number counted from the repository: go-lines, engine-packages, connectors, migrations, api-operations and others in stats.
    <x-page id="page[--section]">text</x-page>A link to another page or section, with the page's title when there is no text.
    <x-include name="file.html"/>A partial.

    Attribute values are matched literally. Write &quot; for a quote inside one, as in start="if is(&quot;worker&quot;) {".

    The page script also understands a few classes: callout drift for spec and code that disagree, callout risk, callout note, evt for an event name, stepper with stage items whose data-lit lights the diagram groups marked data-stage, and data-go="page" on any diagram group to make it open that page.

    Keeping it current#

    Run these from the repository root:

    CommandWhat it does
    make atlasBuilds docs/atlas/site/index.html and docs/atlas/dist/artifact.html, and prints every reference that no longer resolves.
    make atlas-staleLists each written page and how many commits have touched its sources since it was checked, with the files.
    node docs/atlas/atlas.mjs checkBuilds in memory and fails if any reference is broken. Use it before committing.

    To bring a page up to date: run make atlas-stale, read the diff of the listed files since the page's verified commit, change what the page says, set verified to the commit you checked, then rebuild. Code excerpts and line links update themselves. Prose, tables and diagrams are what need a person.

    What the checks cannot see

    An excerpt anchored on a symbol keeps working when the code around it changes. A broken anchor is reported, but a change in meaning is not. And a later migration that redefines a SQL function is not noticed while the old migration still exists. That is why each page also lists its sources and turns amber when they change.

    Publishing#

    site/index.html is the atlas. Commit it with the change that updated a page. dist/artifact.html is the same atlas without the document wrapper, for hosts that add their own, such as a claude.ai artifact. It is not committed.
